Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 9 periods = 360 minutes
Total: 9 periods · 6h 0min

periods.activity_title: From Repeated Addition to Fraction Multiplication

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 1, section 8.1 p.176
textbook_items_in_class.description: A farmer distributes 2/3 acre of land to each of her 5 grandchildren. Total land given = 5 × 2/3 = 10/3 acres.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1–Q4, section 8.1 p.176
textbook_items_in_class.description: Contextual whole-number × fraction problems: (Q1) Tenzin drinks 1/2 glass of milk daily — glasses in a week and in January; (Q2) workers make 1 km of canal in 8 days — km in 1 day and in 5-day week; (Q3) Manju and 2 neighbours share 5 litres of oil among 3 families — oil per family per week and in 4 weeks; (Q4) Moon sets 5/6 hour later each day — hours after 10 pm on Thursday.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 8.1 p.177
homework.description: Multiply and convert to mixed fractions: (a) 7 × 3/5; (b) 4 × 1/3; (c) 9 × 6/7; (d) 13 × 6/11.

time_bands.activity: Open with a number-line sketch on the board showing repeated jumps of equal size. Students recall that 3 × 2 means three jumps of 2 and that the same logic extends to fraction-sized jumps — a quick mental warm-up leading to the question: what does 5 × 2/3 mean on a number line?

Work through Example 1, section 8.1 p.176 ("A farmer distributes 2/3 acre of land to each of her 5 grandchildren....") aloud with the class. Develop the two-step procedure — divide the multiplicand by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator — and show the result 10/3 on the number line.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1–Q4, section 8.1 p.176 ("Contextual whole-number × fraction problems: Tenzin drinks 1/2 glass of milk daily....") in pairs. Encourage students to write the multiplication sentence first, then apply the two-step procedure.
Pairs share answers for one question each. Class discusses whether the product is larger or smaller than the whole-number factor and why, connecting the answer back to the number-line model.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who multiply numerator and denominator both by the whole number — the two-step procedure (÷ denominator, then × numerator) guards against this error. Example 1 (p.176) is the anchor for the class discussion; Example 2, section 8.1 p.176 ("1¼ hours of internet time costs ₹8 per hour....") is an ideal self-study follow-up for students who finish early.

periods.activity_title: Building the Unit-Square Model for Fraction × Fraction

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.180
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the following products using a unit square as the whole: (a) 1/3 × 1/5; (b) 1/4 × 1/3; (c) 1/5 × 1/2; (d) 1/6 × 1/5. Then find 1/12 × 1/18 without drawing.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 8.1 p.181
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the following products using a unit square: (a) 2/3 × 4/5; (b) 1/4 × 2/3; (c) 3/5 × 1/2; (d) 4/6 × 3/5.

time_bands.activity: Draw a unit square on the board. Divide it first into 5 equal columns (each column = 1/5 of the square), then shade 2 columns. Ask students to name the shaded area (2/5). Now divide the shaded region into 4 equal horizontal strips — what is one strip?

Guide students to see that dividing 2/5 into 4 equal parts gives 2/20, and that taking 3 of these gives 6/20. Connect this area argument to the general formula a/b × c/d = (a×c)/(b×d), and introduce cancellation of common factors (apavartana) with a brief historical note about Umasvati (c. 150 CE). Students record the formula and one cancellation example in their notebooks.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.180 ("Find the following products using a unit square....") individually, sketching unit squares for parts (a)–(d) and then attempting the final part without drawing. Those who finish move on to Figure it Out Q2, section 8.1 p.181 ("Find the following products using a unit square...."), applying cancellation before multiplying.

Class-wide check: teacher invites a student to explain why the formula a/b × c/d = (a×c)/(b×d) is shown by the area model. Highlight the commutativity argument — rotating the rectangle gives the same area.

periods.teacher_notes: A common slip is to add denominators rather than multiply them — the unit-square diagram makes this error visible. The Math Talk, section 8.1 p.179 ("Use the unit-square model to multiply 5/4 × 3/2....") is an excellent self-study pointer for students ready to extend the model to fractions greater than 1.

periods.activity_title: Applying Fraction Multiplication in Real Contexts

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.183
textbook_items_in_class.description: A tap fills 7/10 of a tank in 1 hour. Find the fraction filled if the tap runs for: (a) 1/3 hour; (b) 2/3 hour; (c) 3/4 hour; (d) 7/10 hour; (e) how long must the tap run to fill the tank completely?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Try This Q2, section 8.1 p.183
textbook_items_in_class.description: The government takes 1/6 of Somu's land for a road. She gives half the remainder to daughter Krishna and 1/3 of the remainder to son Bora. Find the fraction of original land received by (a) Krishna; (b) Bora; (c) Somu herself.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3–Q5, section 8.1 p.183–184
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the area of a rectangle with sides 3¾ ft and 9⅗ ft (Q3). Tsewang plants 4 saplings with 3/4 m spacing — find first-to-last distance (Q4). Compare 12/15 of 500 g and 3/20 of 4 kg (Q5).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out (product comparison), section 8.1 p.185
homework.description: Explore when the product of two numbers is greater than both, between the two, or less than both. Classify into situations based on whether each factor is between 0 and 1 or greater than 1, fill in the table with examples, and complete the blanks about the relationship.

time_bands.activity: Pose a quick oral problem: if a tap fills 7/10 of a tank per hour, what fraction does it fill in 1/3 of an hour? Students estimate first (more than half or less than half?) before computing.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.183 ("A tap fills 7/10 of a tank in 1 hour....") in pairs. Part (e) — finding the time to fill the tank completely — prompts early discussion of the inverse relationship.
Try This Q2, section 8.1 p.183 ("The government takes 1/6 of Somu's land for a road....") is worked in small groups. Students draw a strip diagram to track successive fractions of the remainder.

Figure it Out Q3–Q5, section 8.1 p.183–184 ("Find the area of a rectangle with sides 3¾ ft and 9⅗ ft....") are attempted individually. Teacher circulates and addresses mixed-number conversion errors. A brief class discussion compares the two quantities in Q5 and asks students which method — common units or fraction multiplication — is more efficient.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often forget to convert mixed numbers to improper fractions before multiplying — encourage them to write the conversion step explicitly. The product-comparison table, Figure it Out (product comparison), section 8.1 p.185, is assigned as homework to prepare for the reasoning work in section 8.2.

periods.activity_title: Division as a Multiplication Question — Building the Reciprocal

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (dividend-divisor-quotient), section 8.2 p.189
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explore the relationship between divisor and quotient: when is the quotient greater than the dividend and when is it less? Connect to the multiplication product-comparison analysis from section 8.1.

time_bands.activity: Write on the board: 6 ÷ 2 = ? means 2 × ? = 6. Ask students to restate 1 ÷ 2/3 = ? as a multiplication question in the same way. Take three or four student responses and write them all on the board without evaluating.

Work step by step through the four division cases from section 8.2: 1 ÷ 2/3, 3 ÷ 2/3, 1/5 ÷ 1/2, and 2/3 ÷ 3/5. In each case, students identify the number that 'undoes' the divisor — its reciprocal — before the term is named. Record the general rule: dividing by a fraction is equivalent to multiplying by its reciprocal. State Brahmagupta's formula a/b ÷ c/d = (a×d)/(b×c) and attribute it to his Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628 CE) and Bhāskara II's 1150 CE clarification.

Students work through Figure it Out (dividend-divisor-quotient), section 8.2 p.189 ("Explore the relationship between divisor and quotient....") in pairs. They examine several examples, conjecture when the quotient exceeds the dividend and when it falls below, then write a two-sentence justification using the reciprocal rule.

Pairs share their conjectures. Teacher consolidates the symmetry with the multiplication analysis: a divisor between 0 and 1 produces a quotient larger than the dividend; a divisor greater than 1 produces a quotient smaller than the dividend.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established through the product-comparison work that multiplying by a number less than 1 shrinks the result, the same logic now re-appears as division: dividing by a fraction less than 1 enlarges the quotient. Watch for students who invert the dividend rather than the divisor — writing the reciprocal step clearly (flip the divisor, keep the dividend) prevents this.

periods.activity_title: Practising Fraction Division Across Varied Problems

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.3 p.196
Figure it Out Q2, section 8.3 p.196
textbook_items_in_class.description: For each context, choose the correct expression and simplify: (a) Maria uses 1/4 m of lace per bag from 8 m — how many bags? (b) 1/2 m of ribbon makes 8 badges — ribbon per badge? (c) baker needs 1/6 kg flour per loaf with 5 kg available — how many loaves?

time_bands.activity: Quick oral drill: teacher reads three division expressions (e.g., 2 ÷ 1/3, 3/4 ÷ 1/2, 5 ÷ 2/5) and students write only the reciprocal of the divisor on their slates or paper — no full computation yet. This confirms the invert step before multi-step problems begin.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 8.3 p.196 ("Evaluate the following divisions: 3÷4/3; 7/9÷14/4....") individually, applying cancellation before multiplying wherever possible. The last item (2/3 ÷ 1⅜) requires converting the mixed divisor — students flag this step in their working.

Small groups tackle Figure it Out Q2, section 8.3 p.196 ("For each context, choose the correct expression and simplify...."). Groups must first write the division sentence in words, then choose the expression, to avoid choosing multiplication by habit. Groups compare answers and resolve disagreements.

Teacher draws attention to Q2(b) — a division that yields a result smaller than 1 — and asks why. Students connect this to the divisor-quotient relationship: the divisor (8) is greater than 1, so the quotient shrinks.

periods.teacher_notes: A persistent error is forgetting to convert mixed-number divisors to improper fractions before inverting; the last item of Q1 is specifically designed to surface this. Figure it Out Q2, section 8.3 p.196 also builds the habit of writing a word equation before choosing the operation — worth emphasising explicitly.

periods.activity_title: Contextual Problems — Tea, Bricks, and Fountains

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 3, section 8.3 p.190
textbook_items_in_class.description: Leena makes 5 cups of tea using 1/4 litre of milk. Milk per cup = 1/4 ÷ 5 = 1/4 × 1/5 = 1/20 litre.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 4, section 8.3 p.190
textbook_items_in_class.description: Baudhāyana's Śhulbasūtra problem: cover 7½ square units with bricks of side 1/5 unit (area 1/25 sq. units). Number of bricks = 15/2 ÷ 1/25 = 15/2 × 25 = 375/2.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example 5, section 8.3 p.191
textbook_items_in_class.description: Pṛithūdakasvāmī's four-fountains problem: fountains fill a cistern in 1, 1/2, 1/4, 1/5 of a day respectively. Together they fill it 1+2+4+5 = 12 times a day, so the combined fill time is 1/12 day.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (Example 5 blanks), section 8.3 p.191
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete the four-fountains problem (Example 5): compute 1÷1/2, 1÷1/4, 1÷1/5, sum all four values, and confirm total fill time = 1/12 day.

time_bands.activity: Present Example 3, section 8.3 p.190 ("Leena makes 5 cups of tea using 1/4 litre of milk....") as a class. Students translate the problem to a division sentence before seeing the solution, then verify the answer using multiplication: 5 × 1/20 = 1/4.

Work through Example 4, section 8.3 p.190 ("Baudhāyana's Śhulbasūtra problem: cover 7½ square units with bricks of side 1/5 unit....") together. Emphasise converting the mixed number 7½ to 15/2 and the area formula for each brick. Mention Baudhāyana's Śhulbasūtra (c. 800 BCE) briefly as historical context.

Introduce Example 5, section 8.3 p.191 ("Pṛithūdakasvāmī's four-fountains problem....") with the key insight that each fountain's daily contribution is found by 1 ÷ fill-time. Students complete the blanks in Figure it Out (Example 5 blanks), section 8.3 p.191 ("Complete the four-fountains problem: compute 1÷1/2, 1÷1/4, 1÷1/5....") individually, then pair-check.

Class discussion: why does dividing 1 by a fraction less than 1 give a number greater than 1? Students connect this to the fountain's meaning — a fountain that fills the cistern in 1/4 of a day fills it 4 times in a full day.

periods.teacher_notes: Example 4 often confuses students who treat 7½ as two separate numbers; insisting on the improper-fraction conversion before setting up the division is the key checkpoint. Example 5 is rich — students who grasp it early can be challenged to pose their own fountain problem with different fill times.

periods.activity_title: Nested Figures, the Dramma Problem, and Historical Puzzles

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Math Talk, section 8.3 p.192
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the fraction of the whole square that the shaded region occupies in the nested figure (Fig. 8.4). The shaded part is 3/4 of a yellow triangle that is 1/2 of a red square that is 1/4 of the whole: 3/4 × 1/2 × 1/4 = 3/32.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (shaded-region diagrams), section 8.3 p.193
textbook_items_in_class.description: In each of two given figures, find the fraction of the big square that the shaded region occupies (figures (a) and (b) from the nested-square diagrams).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out (Dramma problem), section 8.3 p.193
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete the Bhāskarāchārya dramma problem: evaluate 1/2 × 2/3 × 3/4 × 1/5 × 1/16 × 1/4 of a dramma and convert to cowrie shells (1 dramma = 1280 cowrie shells). Also convert coin denominations using given rates to express 1 cowrie shell in gold dinars.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 8.3 p.197
homework.description: If 1/4 kg of flour makes 12 rotis, how much flour is needed for 6 rotis?

time_bands.activity: Display a large nested-square diagram on the board (redrawn from Fig. 8.4). Students identify the whole, then successively name each nested shape as a fraction of its container. The class works through Math Talk, section 8.3 p.192 ("Find the fraction of the whole square that the shaded region occupies....") together, multiplying the fractions layer by layer.

Students draw their own nested figures — a square containing a rectangle containing a triangle — and shade a portion, then compute the shaded fraction using successive multiplication. They then compare with a partner and attempt Figure it Out (shaded-region diagrams), section 8.3 p.193 ("In each of two given figures, find the fraction of the big square that the shaded region occupies....").

Introduce the Bhāskarāchārya dramma problem through Figure it Out (Dramma problem), section 8.3 p.193 ("Complete the Bhāskarāchārya dramma problem: evaluate 1/2 × 2/3 × 3/4 × 1/5 × 1/16 × 1/4 of a dramma...."). Students work in groups to evaluate the chain of multiplications and then convert the result to cowrie shells, enjoying the historical context.

Groups share their answers. Teacher highlights that cancellation at each step (apavartana) makes the chain product manageable — connecting the historical technique to the algebraic shortcut the class already knows.

periods.teacher_notes: Students sometimes lose track of which fraction is 'of' which in nested figures — insisting they annotate each layer's fraction before multiplying avoids this. The Dramma problem rewards the use of cancellation; students who do not cancel will still reach 1 cowrie shell, but the computation is laborious — a productive comparison to make in the debrief.
materials: Plain paper for drawing nested figures

periods.activity_title: Extended Practice — Mixed Contexts and the Ant-Splitting Puzzle

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 8.3 p.197
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mira reads a 400-page novel: she reads 1/5 of pages yesterday and 3/10 today. How many more pages remain?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q11, section 8.3 p.197
textbook_items_in_class.description: Ant-splitting problem: a colony splits equally at each fork. Find the fraction reaching each food source for successive depths: (1−1/2); (1−1/2)(1−1/3); up to (1−1/2)(1−1/3)(1−1/4)(1−1/5); and (1−1/2)…(1−1/10). Make a general statement and explain.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q12, section 8.3 p.197
textbook_items_in_class.description: Evaluate the telescoping products: 1−1/2; (1−1/2)(1−1/3); (1−1/2)(1−1/3)(1−1/4)(1−1/5); and (1−1/2)(1−1/3)…(1−1/10). Generalise the pattern.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 8.3 p.197
homework.description: Mariam and cousins eat 4/5 of a cake. The remaining cake is shared equally by 3 friends. What fraction of the whole cake does each friend get?

time_bands.activity: Students work individually on Figure it Out Q5, section 8.3 p.197 ("Mira reads a 400-page novel: she reads 1/5 of pages yesterday and 3/10 today...."). After computing, students are asked to verify by adding their answer to the read pages and confirming the total is 400.

Introduce Figure it Out Q11, section 8.3 p.197 ("Ant-splitting problem: a colony splits equally at each fork....") with a diagram of the ant-fork on the board. Small groups compute the fraction reaching the food source for each successive depth, recording their products in a table.

Groups move to Figure it Out Q12, section 8.3 p.197 ("Evaluate the telescoping products: 1−1/2; (1−1/2)(1−1/3)...."). They compute each partial product, enter it in the table, and attempt to state the general pattern — (1−1/2)(1−1/3)…(1−1/n) = 1/n — in their own words before the class reconvenes.
Brief whole-class share: one group states the pattern, another explains why it works using the fact that each factor (1−1/k) = (k−1)/k, so adjacent numerators and denominators cancel.

periods.teacher_notes: The telescoping product is the chapter's most open-ended reasoning challenge; students who see cancellation quickly will race ahead — ask them to write an explanation accessible to a classmate who has not yet spotted the pattern. Figure it Out Q8, section 8.3 p.197, assigned as homework, revisits the 'fraction of a remainder' structure from section 8.1's land problem, consolidating the full chapter arc.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis — Connecting Multiplication, Division, and Pattern

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 8.3 p.197
Figure it Out Q4, section 8.3 p.197
textbook_items_in_class.description: Pāṭīgaṇita problem (Sridharacharya, 9th century CE): find the sum 1÷1/6 + 1÷1/10 + 1÷1/13 + 1÷1/9 + 1÷1/2.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q10, section 8.3 p.197
textbook_items_in_class.description: What fraction of the whole square is the shaded region in the given nested diagram?

time_bands.activity: Open with Figure it Out Q9, section 8.3 p.197 ("Choose all correct descriptions of the product (565/465) × (707/676)....") as a no-computation challenge: students must decide all correct options using only the product-comparison principles established in sections 8.1 and 8.2 — whether each factor is greater than 1 or between 0 and 1. Discuss as a class.

Students work through Figure it Out Q4, section 8.3 p.197 ("Pāṭīgaṇita problem (Sridharacharya, 9th century CE): find the sum 1÷1/6 + 1÷1/10 + 1÷1/13 + 1÷1/9 + 1÷1/2....") in pairs. Each division requires applying the reciprocal rule, and then the five results must be added — a problem that knits together the division procedure and fraction addition.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q10, section 8.3 p.197 ("What fraction of the whole square is the shaded region in the given nested diagram?...") individually, using the successive-multiplication approach from the nested-figure work. The result is compared with the 3/32 answer from the Math Talk (section 8.3 p.192) to check whether the structure is the same or different.

Class discussion synthesises the chapter: teacher draws a three-column table on the board — Multiplication, Division, Pattern — and invites students to contribute one key idea or method to each column from their own working across the chapter. The reciprocal link, the area model, the product-comparison rule, and the telescoping cancellation are named and placed by students, closing the chapter on student-generated language.

periods.teacher_notes: Q9 is a deliberate reasoning exercise: students who attempt to compute (565/465) × (707/676) numerically are missing the point — redirect them to compare each factor with 1. The Sridharacharya problem (Q4) can be checked by summing the five whole-number results and verifying that the answer is a recognisable number, giving students a self-check without the teacher needing to intervene.

items.prompt: A worker builds 1/3 km of road each day. Which expression gives the total distance built in 6 days, and what is its value?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the whole number by the numerator and divide by the denominator: 6 × 1 ÷ 3 = 2.

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student added the whole number and the fraction instead of multiplying, treating × as +.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student divided by the fraction rather than multiplying, confusing the operation.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student applied the two-step procedure in reverse order — dividing numerator by whole number — giving 1/2 instead of 2.

inclusivity.support: Sketch equal jumps of 1/3 on a number line and count 6 jumps to reach the answer.
inclusivity.challenge: Write a different real-life sentence that gives the same multiplication, then solve it.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1–Q4, section 8.1 p.176
exercise.description: Contextual whole-number × fraction problems: (Q1) Tenzin drinks 1/2 glass of milk daily — glasses in a week and in January; (Q2) workers make 1 km of canal in 8 days — km in 1 day and in 5-day week; (Q3) Manju and 2 neighbours share 5 litres of oil among 3 families — oil per family per week and in 4 weeks; (Q4) Moon sets 5/6 hour later each day — hours after 10 pm on Thursday.

items.prompt: Using the unit-square area model, what is the product of 1/4 and 1/5?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the formula a/b × c/d = (a×c)/(b×d): numerators multiply and denominators multiply.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student added the denominators (4+5=9) and kept numerator 1, confusing addition with multiplication.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added numerators and multiplied denominators, or performed a mixed operation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student added both numerators and both denominators separately, treating the product like a fraction addition.

inclusivity.support: Draw a unit square, divide into 4 equal columns and 5 equal rows, then count how many small cells 1 column and 1 row share.
inclusivity.challenge: Without drawing, state the product of 1/12 × 1/18 and explain why the denominator grows so quickly.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.180
exercise.description: Find the following products using a unit square as the whole: (a) 1/3 × 1/5; (b) 1/4 × 1/3; (c) 1/5 × 1/2; (d) 1/6 × 1/5. Then find 1/12 × 1/18 without drawing.

items.prompt: Riya says: 'When I divide 3 by a number, the answer is always less than 3.' Priya says: 'That is not always true for fractions.' Who is correct? Justify your answer using the reciprocal rule and one numerical example.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya is correct. When the divisor is a fraction between 0 and 1, the quotient exceeds the dividend. For example, 3 ÷ 1/2 = 3 × 2 = 6, which is greater than 3. The reciprocal rule shows that dividing by 1/2 is the same as multiplying by 2, so the result grows.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Restate division as multiplication by the reciprocal: 3 ÷ (c/d) = 3 × (d/c); when d > c the product exceeds 3.

inclusivity.support: Pair-share first: ask your partner 'What does 3 ÷ 1/2 mean in words?' before writing your answer.
inclusivity.challenge: Alter the claim: what if the divisor equals exactly 1? Or is greater than 1? Re-explain both cases.

exercise.description: Explore the relationship between divisor and quotient: when is the quotient greater than the dividend and when is it less? Connect to the multiplication product-comparison analysis from section 8.1.

items.prompt: A tap fills 3/5 of a tank in one hour. What fraction of the tank is filled if the tap runs for 2/3 of an hour? Show your working.

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the two fractions using a/b × c/d = (a×c)/(b×d), then cancel common factors to simplify.

inclusivity.support: Draw a strip representing 1 full tank, shade 3/5, then shade 2/3 of that shaded part.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the running time to 4/3 hours and find the fraction filled; explain why the answer now exceeds 3/5.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.1 p.183
exercise.description: A tap fills 7/10 of a tank in 1 hour. Find the fraction filled if the tap runs for: (a) 1/3 hour; (b) 2/3 hour; (c) 3/4 hour; (d) 7/10 hour; (e) how long must the tap run to fill the tank completely?

items.prompt: A baker has 5/6 kg of flour. Each loaf of bread needs 1/4 kg of flour. How many complete loaves can the baker make? Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 3 complete loaves. Working: 5/6 ÷ 1/4 = 5/6 × 4/1 = 20/6 = 10/3 = 3 and 1/3. Since only complete loaves count, the answer is 3.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide by multiplying by the reciprocal: 5/6 × 4 = 20/6 = 10/3; take the whole-number part for complete loaves.

inclusivity.support: Represent 5/6 kg on a number-line strip and mark off portions of 1/4 kg one at a time.
inclusivity.challenge: If the baker also has 1/3 kg of a second flour, how many complete loaves can be made in total from both portions?

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 8.3 p.196

items.prompt: Two pipes fill a tank: Pipe A fills the tank in 1/3 of a day, and Pipe B fills it in 1/4 of a day. How many times does each pipe fill the tank in one full day? How many times do both pipes together fill the tank in one full day, and what is their combined fill time?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Pipe A fills the tank 1 ÷ 1/3 = 3 times a day. Pipe B fills it 1 ÷ 1/4 = 4 times a day. Together they fill it 3 + 4 = 7 times a day. Combined fill time = 1/7 of a day.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find each pipe's daily rate by dividing 1 by its fill-time fraction, sum the rates, then take the reciprocal for the combined fill time.

inclusivity.support: Draw a bar for one full day and shade the portion each pipe fills in its given time to see the rate visually.
inclusivity.challenge: Add a third pipe that fills the tank in 1/6 of a day and recalculate the combined fill time.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out (Example 5 blanks), section 8.3 p.191
exercise.description: Complete the four-fountains problem (Example 5): compute 1÷1/2, 1÷1/4, 1÷1/5, sum all four values, and confirm total fill time = 1/12 day.

items.prompt: A large square contains a smaller square that is 1/3 of its area. Inside the smaller square is a triangle that is 1/2 of the smaller square's area. A shaded region inside the triangle is 2/3 of the triangle's area. What fraction of the large square is the shaded region?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply the successive fractions layer by layer: 1/3 × 1/2 × 2/3 = 2/18 = 1/9.

inclusivity.support: Draw and label each nested shape before multiplying, annotating what fraction each is of its container.
inclusivity.challenge: Add a fourth level: a dot inside the shaded region covers 1/4 of it. What fraction of the whole square is the dot?

exercise.description: Find the fraction of the whole square that the shaded region occupies in the nested figure (Fig. 8.4). The shaded part is 3/4 of a yellow triangle that is 1/2 of a red square that is 1/4 of the whole: 3/4 × 1/2 × 1/4 = 3/32.

items.prompt: Aditya has a 240-page book. He reads 1/4 of the pages on Saturday and 1/3 of the pages on Sunday. How many pages remain unread?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 100 pages remain. Working: Pages read Saturday = 1/4 × 240 = 60. Pages read Sunday = 1/3 × 240 = 80. Total read = 60 + 80 = 140. Remaining = 240 − 140 = 100.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find each day's pages by multiplying the fraction by 240, sum them, and subtract from 240.

inclusivity.support: Represent 240 pages as a strip diagram; shade Saturday's portion then Sunday's portion before counting the unshaded part.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the total to 360 pages and the fractions to 2/5 and 1/6; find the remaining pages and verify your answer using a different order of operations.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 8.3 p.197
exercise.description: Mira reads a 400-page novel: she reads 1/5 of pages yesterday and 3/10 today. How many more pages remain?

items.prompt: Both fractions in the product (7/8) × (11/13) are between 0 and 1. Which of the following statements correctly describes the product?

options.label: A
options.text: The product equals 7/8 because multiplication preserves one factor.

options.label: C
options.text: The product is greater than both 7/8 and 11/13.

options.label: D
options.text: The product is less than both 7/8 and 11/13.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: B — when both factors are between 0 and 1, their product is less than either factor. Here (7/8) × (11/13) = 77/104, which is less than 7/8 (= 91/104) and less than 11/13 (= 88/104).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the product-comparison principle: multiplying by a number between 0 and 1 shrinks the other factor.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student believes multiplication always makes numbers larger, forgetting the rule for factors less than 1.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks one factor is unchanged by multiplication, confusing multiplication with an identity operation.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has not considered that two fractions less than 1 multiplied together cannot exceed 1.

inclusivity.support: Refer back to the product-comparison table in your textbook and find the row where both factors are between 0 and 1.
inclusivity.challenge: Change one factor to a value greater than 1, say 7/8 × 14/13, and re-determine all correct descriptions of the product.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 8.3 p.197
